articles.title: Does `docker compose down` Delete Your Data?
articles.excerpt: Two commands can have very different consequences for your database: docker compose down docker compose down --volumes The difference comes down to how Docker Compose manages volumes. Consider this Po…
articles.body: Two commands can have very different consequences for your database: docker compose down docker compose down --volumes The difference comes down to how Docker Compose manages volumes. Containers are temporary. Named volumes persist. Consider this PostgreSQL configuration: services : db : image : postgres:17 environment : POSTGRES_PASSWORD : ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set a password} volumes : - db_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data volumes : db_data : The database files live in db_data , a named volume with a lifecycle separate from the container. Running docker compose down removes the containers and project networks, but keeps the named volume. Starting the same project again with docker compose up -d reuses the existing data. Adding --volumes requests removal of the project’s managed volumes too.

articles.title: A Voice Signature Is Not Blanket Consent
articles.excerpt: A Voice Signature Is Not Blanket Consent A cryptographic signature can prove that a particular key approved a particular payload. That is valuable. It is also much narrower than the claim many voice-A…
articles.body: A Voice Signature Is Not Blanket Consent A cryptographic signature can prove that a particular key approved a particular payload. That is valuable. It is also much narrower than the claim many voice-AI systems need to make. A signed audio record does not automatically prove that the person behind the voice agreed to this model, this buyer, this campaign, this territory, this duration, or this revenue arrangement. It does not prove that a past approval remains live after the person withdraws it. For a serious voice economy, we have to stop collapsing those claims into one technical artifact. Evidence is necessary, but it has a scope Voice platforms are rightly investing in hashes, watermarks, provenance metadata, and signatures. Each can answer a useful question.

articles.title: What Is Clean Code? A Guide to Principles and Best Practices
articles.excerpt: Writing code is like giving a speech. If you use too many big words, you confuse your audience. Define every word, and you end up putting your audience to sleep. Similarly, when you write code, follow…
articles.body: Writing code is like giving a speech. If you use too many big words, you confuse your audience. Define every word, and you end up putting your audience to sleep. Similarly, when you write code, following clean code rules makes sure it is readable, understandable, and maintainable for future readers. To paraphrase software engineer Martin Fowler, "Anybody can write code that a computer can understand. Good programmers write code that humans can understand." As software developers, understanding how to write clean code that is functional, easy to read, and adheres to best practices helps you create better software consistently. This article discusses what clean code is and why it's essential. It also provides principles and best practices for writing clean and maintainable code.

articles.excerpt: Two leading space scientists say there is a need to redefine the edge of the solar system based on the Milky Way's gravity, including its dark matter.
articles.body: Two leading space scientists say there is a need to redefine the edge of the solar system by presenting a theory which states that measurements of the Milky Way's gravitational field, including its dark matter, redraws the sun's frontier. That theory was put forward by Jim Green, former NASA chief scientist and past director of the space agency's Planetary Science Division, along with Ed Belbruno, a professor of mathematics at Yeshiva University and a senior research associate at Princeton University. The solar system's gravitational frontier extends to nearly 3.8 light-years from the sun , they contend, roughly 241,000 astronomical units (AU), a distance that brings the "edge" of the solar system to within the same scale as the separation between neighboring stars.
